hall.qa: The Weapon X program transforms Kane into a cyborg, grafting cybernetic arms in place of his real ones.
hall.qb: …this run, both her arms were cut off by Hydra member Gorgon, and were later replaced with two prosthetic arms.
hall.note: Both lost their arms and got artificial ones: Weapon X grafts cybernetic arms onto Kane, and Yo-Yo's are cut off by Hydra's Gorgon and replaced. In the link network there is no path between them at all.

hall.qa: …DeFilippis intended for the character to commit suicide early in the series after coming out as gay and finding himself rejected by his family and friends.
hall.qb: …a brief appearance in GLA #2 written by Dan Slott, in which Living Lightning is revealed to be gay.
hall.note: Two of Marvel's gay characters, and both pages tell the story of them coming out. Three hops apart and never linked.

hall.qa: …Eagle kills Golden Archer with his mace, but loses the use of his wings after Lamprey drains the artificial gravity effect from them.
hall.qb: The birds raised him as their own, and gave him artificial wings.
hall.note: Two flyers on artificial wings: Blue Eagle falls when Lamprey drains his wings' artificial gravity, and Red Raven's were a gift from the Bird People. Four hops apart.

hall.qa: Morbius (born Michael Morbius, also known as Morbius the Living Vampire) is a character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.
hall.qb: During his adventures as a member of Freedom's Five, he encounters the mysterious Baron Blood, a vampire saboteur for the Germans.
hall.note: Morbius is the Living Vampire. Union Jack's page is about World War I and Baron Blood, a vampire who turns out to be a Falsworth himself. A real shared theme from two different eras.

hall.qa: …for anthology Warrior, without permission to do so from Mick Anglo, who was still owner of the rights to the character.
hall.qb: Marvel had originally hoped to license the television series Kung Fu, but the rights were unavailable, and the character was instead spun off from novelist Sax Rohmer's licensed pulp villain Fu Manchu…
hall.note: Not the stories but the paperwork: both pages tell a rights saga (who owned Miracleman; Marvel wanted Kung Fu, couldn't get it, and made Shang-Chi instead).

hall.qa: Bird-Brain is a character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics, primarily in association with the New Mutants.
hall.qb: Brain Drain (Werner Schmidt) is a character appearing in American comic books published by Marvel Comics.
hall.note: 98% of the match is the word brain. Both names contain it, and brain is lowercase often enough elsewhere that our name filter keeps it. A pun, not a twin.

hall.qa: Born in the present-day, Nathan was infected with a deadly techno-organic virus as an infant and was sent into a possible future timeline where his condition could be stabilized.
hall.qb: Soon after, Ogre is knocked unconscious by Techno, a former member of the Thunderbolts.
hall.note: Cable has a techno-organic virus, and Ogre gets knocked out by a villain called Techno. The tokenizer split techno-organic, and one word glued two unrelated pages together.
